tools.name: minerva_cad_references
tools.description: List the foreign mesh files (glTF/GLB placed by the .mcad mesh() primitive) currently mounted in a live CAD editor: each reference's name, the path the source wrote, the resolved path, its composed 4x4 pose, and its bounding box plus the bounding box of every node inside it. Every box is millimetres in BOTH frames: 'local' is the reference's own converted frame — millimetres, Z-up, with the mesh() pose taken back off (the numbers to write back into the DSL; the file's raw units and axis convention have already been applied) and 'world' is the posed CAD scene (the numbers to compare against the evaluated solid). Every reference the source named appears here whether or not its file could be read: 'status' is ok, missing, unsupported, unreadable, empty, oversize or unresolved, 'reason' names the file and says what went wrong, and a failed reference is drawn in the world as a wireframe marker at its pose. 'triangle_count', 'bytes' and 'outlines_skipped' report size; a mesh over the outline budget renders shaded without ortho outlines. This verb describes the REFERENCES; minerva_cad_get_mesh_info describes the evaluated solid.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

tools.name: minerva_cad_find_holes
tools.description: Find and MEASURE the holes in a mounted reference mesh. Works in two stages: candidates are proposed by segmenting the mesh and fitting cylinders to it (no seed, no preferred axis — a hole drilled at an angle is found the same way an axis-aligned one is), then every candidate is verified against physics colliders with a ray-sampled gauge pin: rays leave the pin's axis at 24 azimuths from each of 5 stations along its length, so the verification is a SAMPLE of the wall and not a volumetric proof — a feature standing between two rays can be missed, and at a 5 mm radius 15° of arc is 1.3 mm of unsampled wall. Returns for each hole: center_mm {world, local}, axis {world, local}, dia_mm (the diameter the tessellation's circumscribed circle implies), gauge_dia_mm (the largest pin the sampled rays allow — smaller than dia_mm by the facet chord, which is why both are reported; gauge_bounded is false when no wall was met inside the search bound, and then gauge_dia_mm is 0 and gauge_dia_at_least_mm carries the floor the bound implies), inscribed_dia_mm, facets, coverage, residual_mm, through (true only when a ray passes all the way along the axis — a blind pocket looks identical to a fitter), depth_mm, verified, and source ('fit', or 'ray-grid' when the fitter found nothing and a ray-grid seed was used instead). A hole that passes through several nodes of the same file (a board's substrate, copper and mask, say) is reported ONCE, with 'nodes' listing every node it crosses and 'node' naming the first. Millimetres throughout.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

reference.description: Restrict to the reference of this name (as bound in the DSL). Default: every mounted reference.

node.description: Restrict to one node inside the file, as named by minerva_cad_references.

min_dia_mm.description: Smallest hole diameter to report. Default 0.3.

max_dia_mm.description: Largest hole diameter to report. Default 30.

min_coverage.description: How much of a full turn the wall must cover to count as a hole rather than a fillet, 0..1. Default 0.6.

region_angle_deg.description: Normal-continuity angle used to segment the mesh. Raise it for a coarsely tessellated file (fewer than about 16 facets per circle). Default 25.

verified_only.description: Drop candidates the gauge could not confirm. Default false — an unverified candidate is information.

fallback.description: Fall back to a ray-grid seed when the fitter proposes nothing. Default true.

axis.description: Direction the ray-grid fallback drills along, [x, y, z] in world millimetres. Default [0, 0, 1]. The fitter itself needs no axis — this only aims the fallback grid.

pitch_mm.description: Spacing of the ray-grid fallback, in millimetres. Default 1. A hole narrower than the pitch can be missed; halving the pitch quadruples the number of rays.

tools.name: minerva_cad_find_cylinders
tools.description: Like minerva_cad_find_holes but for cylindrical features of either sense: kind='concave' is bores and holes, kind='convex' is bosses, standoffs and pins, kind='any' is both. Concave candidates are verified with a gauge pin; convex ones are verified by contact with the wall: a probe straddling the fitted radius must touch it and a probe standing off that radius must touch nothing (a trimesh collider is a surface, so 'is there material inside' is not a question physics can answer). Same reported shape as find_holes, plus form ('concave'/'convex').

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

reference.description: Restrict to the reference of this name.

node.description: Restrict to one node inside the file.

kind.description: Which sense of cylinder to report. Default 'any'.

min_coverage.description: Minimum fraction of a full turn the surface covers, 0..1.

region_angle_deg.description: Normal-continuity angle used to segment the mesh. Default 25.

tools.name: minerva_cad_gauge
tools.description: Put a gauge of a given size at a given place in the posed CAD world and ask whether it fits. shape='cylinder' is a pin (dia_mm + length_mm, pointing along axis), 'box' is a block (size_mm [x,y,z]), 'sphere' is a ball (dia_mm). Returns {fits, contacts[{point_mm {world, local}, node, reference}], clearance_mm, clearance_bound_mm, clearance_bounded}. The gauge is RAY-SAMPLED, not volumetric: rays leave it at 24 azimuths from each of 5 stations along its length (plus its two ends), so 'it fits' means nothing was found on those rays — a rib or a burr between two of them can be missed. A gauge that does not fit reports where it touched, so 'why will this screw not go in' has an answer with coordinates. In open space no ray meets a wall at all: clearance_bounded is then false and the room is reported as clearance_at_least_mm, the search bound, which is a floor and not a measurement. Positions are millimetres in the posed world frame; at_mm is world.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

dia_mm.description: Diameter for cylinder and sphere gauges.

length_mm.description: Length of a cylinder gauge along its axis. Default 5.

size_mm.description: Box gauge size [x, y, z] in millimetres.

at_mm.description: Gauge centre [x, y, z] in posed world millimetres.

reference.description: Report contact points in this reference's local frame as well. Default: the reference each contact itself lies on. A contact that cannot be attributed to a reference is reported in world only, with local null and local_unavailable saying why — no reference is guessed.

tools.name: minerva_cad_probe
tools.description: What is under this pixel? Casts a ray from the named pane's camera through the given pixel of that pane and returns the first surface it meets: {hit, position_mm {world, local}, normal, reference, node}. Pixels are the pane's own, top-left origin, in the size reported by width_px/height_px — the same frame a minerva_cad_snapshot of that pane has before any max_edge downscale. This is how a point on a picture becomes a number.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

view.description: Which pane the pixel is in. Default 'active'. In narrow layout only one pane renders, so a named pane is REFUSED with a reason rather than answered from the pane that happens to be showing — use 'active' there, as minerva_cad_snapshot requires.

px.description: [x, y] pixel in that pane, top-left origin.

tools.name: minerva_cad_view_overlay
tools.description: Draw a millimetre grid on the CAD floor and/or the three world axes through the origin, in every pane, and report each pane's scale: {px_per_mm, origin_px, width_px, height_px, projection}. px_per_mm is a real number for the orthographic panes (top/front/right) and null for the iso pane, which is a perspective projection and has no single scale. The overlay is scene geometry, so the picture is still taken with minerva_cad_snapshot — call this first and the snapshot comes back with a ruler in it. overlay='none' clears it. In narrow layout the four named panes do not exist, so 'views' holds the one pane that renders and 'views_unavailable' says why the others are missing.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

grid_mm.description: Requested grid spacing in millimetres. Doubled as needed to keep the grid readable; the spacing actually drawn is returned. Default 10.

tools.name: minerva_cad_get_selected_reference
tools.description: What the user last pointed at on a reference mesh — the sibling of minerva_cad_get_selected_edge for foreign geometry. Returns {selected, reference, node, point_mm {world, local}, normal, bounds_mm {local, world}, size_mm, view, px, nearest_hole}. The click is the handoff: the user knows which bracket or which hole they mean and cannot say it in millimetres, so read this before measuring and you measure the thing they pointed at. point_mm.local is the reference's own converted frame — millimetres, Z-up, with the mesh() pose taken back off (what you write into the .mcad, because the pose is applied on top of it); point_mm.world is the posed scene. nearest_hole is the FITTED hole the point lies inside, if any — a hypothesis, not a measurement; minerva_cad_find_holes gauges it. stale=true means the document no longer mounts that reference.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

include_hole.description: Look for the fitted hole the selected point lies inside. Costs one segmentation pass on the first call for a file, cached afterwards. Default true.

tools.name: minerva_cad_select_reference
tools.description: Select a reference node from here, the way a user selects one by clicking it in a view: it highlights in the panel's reference list and becomes what minerva_cad_get_selected_reference returns. Use it to point at a node you found by name so the user can see which one you mean. With no point_mm the selection sits at the centre of the node's bounds; give point_mm (in the reference's own frame) to point at a specific spot. Returns the same payload as minerva_cad_get_selected_reference.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

reference.description: Reference name, as reported by minerva_cad_references.

node.description: Node inside that reference (references[].nodes[].name). Defaults to its first node.

point_mm.description: [x, y, z] in the REFERENCE's own frame, not the world. Optional.

include_hole.description: Look for the fitted hole the point lies inside. Default true.

tools.name: minerva_cad_view_state
tools.description: Read-only snapshot of what the user is currently looking at in a live CAD editor: the responsive layout class (xs/sm/md/lg/xl), the active viewport pane id (top/front/right/iso in wide layout, or the narrow-layout single pane), the narrow-layout projection dropdown selection, and the active pane camera's orientation/zoom (view_preset, target [x,y,z] in mm, distance, yaw, pitch). Use this for SEE-context before deciding whether a minerva_cad_snapshot is worth taking, or to confirm which pane a snapshot view="active" call would capture.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

skills.title: CAD modeling with the .mcad DSL
skills.summary: Author and edit .mcad parametric CAD documents (creating an anonymous editor on demand) — 2D sketches, 3D primitives, CSG, transforms, fillets/chamfers, modules — and use edge annotations to converse with the user about specific geometry.
skills.preconditions: A .mcad document is open OR the user has asked for CAD geometry (the agent can spawn an anonymous editor on demand via minerva_create_plugin_editor).
skills.outcome: The .mcad source produces the geometry the user described. Translator errors are surfaced verbatim. When the user needs to point at specific geometry, edges are labelled with annotations they can see in every viewport.
skills.steps:
0. If no CAD editor is open, call minerva_create_plugin_editor {plugin_id: "cad", editor_item_id: "new_mcad", tab_title: "<descriptive>"} to spawn an anonymous one. Use the returned editor_name as the key for steps 1–6. Ask the user to click the point BEFORE arming any annotation tool: while a tool is armed the annotation overlay captures every click and no reference point can be picked.
1. Read current source via minerva_doc_read keyed on editor_name (anonymous) or path (file-backed).
2. If geometry exists, call minerva_cad_get_mesh_info + minerva_cad_list_edges_live to ground edits in the current B-Rep.
3. When the user references edges they labeled ("the edges I pinned", "these edges"), call minerva_cad_list_user_labels FIRST and operate on every edge_id returned (multi-edge requests need ALL of them, not just the most-recent click). To ASK "which edge?", label candidates yourself with minerva_cad_annotate_edges; if the user clicks one, read minerva_cad_get_selected_edge.
4. Replace source with minerva_doc_write {editor_name, text: <full new source>}; the panel auto-evaluates. NEVER use minerva_doc_edit on CAD editors — string-replace doesn't apply to plugin-scene documents; always doc_write the full new source.
5. Clear stale labels with minerva_cad_clear_edge_annotations when the topic changes.
6. Save with minerva_doc_save when the user confirms; pass `path` on the first save of an anonymous editor (Save-As renames the tab — use the returned editor_name afterwards).
skills.system_prompt:
§0 — MCAD vs OpenSCAD habits (read FIRST)

MCAD looks like OpenSCAD but is not OpenSCAD. The worker DOES accept cylinder(h=, r=, center=true) and the boolean operators &&, ||, !. It DOES NOT accept //, /* */, trailing semicolons, sphere(d=), or OpenSCAD union() {...} blocks.

OpenSCAD habits to drop:
- // and /* */ comments → use # only.
- ; at end of statements → never. One statement per line.
- sphere(d=10) → use sphere(5) (radius). No diameter keyword.
- union() { a; b; } / difference() { a - b; } → use a + b and a - b operators.
- module foo() { return shape; } with braces → Python-ish module foo(): ... return shape.

If you find yourself writing //, ;, sphere(d=, or a { — STOP. Re-read §1.

§1 — DSL vocabulary (vetted against canonical .mcad examples)

.mcad is indentation-aware (Python-style). The build123d/OCCT worker evaluates it into a B-Rep solid plus an indexed edge registry.

Variables and arithmetic:
  height = 100
  width = 80
  thickness = 10

2D primitives — used inside `sketch:` blocks:
  rect(w, h)
  circle(r)
  oval(w, h)
  polygon(points)

3D primitives:
  cube(x, y, z)                                # axis-aligned box, CORNER AT ORIGIN — extents [0,0,0]→[x,y,z]. To centre: translate([-x/2,-y/2,-z/2], cube(x,y,z))
  sphere(r)                                    # radius — no d= keyword. CENTRED at origin.
  cylinder(r, h)                               # positional. Axis along +Z. Without center=true the base sits at z=0 and the top at z=h.
  cylinder(h=H, r=R, center=true)              # keyword form (canonical examples use this when translating/rotating cylinders)
  cylinder(h=H, r1=BIG, r2=SMALL, center=true) # truncated cone

CSG operators:
  a + b   # union (fuse)
  a - b   # difference (cut)
No * intersection operator.

Transforms — function form with array vector:
  translate([x, y, z], shape)
  rotate([rx, ry, rz], shape)   # degrees about each axis
  scale([sx, sy, sz], shape)
  mirror([nx, ny, nz], shape)

Reference meshes — a foreign file placed in the scene, never altered (see §12):
  board = mesh("boards/main.glb")                     # path recorded verbatim; the panel resolves it against the .mcad file
  board = translate([0, 0, 5], rotate([0, 0, 90], mesh("main.glb")))
  part  = mesh("scan.stl", units="mm", up="z")        # units/up override the format default

2D positioning sugar inside sketch: blocks:
  rect(w, h) center at point(x, y)

Operations:
  extrude(profile, length)
  fillet shape, [<edge_idx>, ...], r=R    # PREFERRED: list form. All ids resolved against the current registry, applied in ONE OCCT op.
  fillet shape, <edge_idx>, r=R           # single-edge form. SAFE only as a one-off — see §11 before chaining.
  chamfer shape, [<edge_idx>, ...], d=D   # PREFERRED list form (note: distance keyword is `d=`, not `c=`).
  chamfer shape, <edge_idx>, d=D          # single-edge form. Same caveat as fillet.
  shell shape, thickness               # postfix; mutates `shape` in place
  loft:                                # block — see §2
      z=N: profile_expr
      ...

Export:
  export name "filename.{stl|3mf|step}"

§2 — Language constructs

`sketch:` blocks are ANONYMOUS. Bind named 2D shapes inside, combine with +/-, then `extrude` references the inner variable by name:

  sketch:
      flange = rect(width, thickness) center at point(0, height - thickness / 2)
      web    = rect(thickness, height - thickness) center at point(0, (height - thickness) / 2)
      profile = flange + web

  beam = extrude(profile, length)

CRITICAL: do NOT write `sketch <name>:` — sketches don't take a name. Do NOT put bare `rect(...)` lines without `name = rect(...)` — the block needs named profiles to compose.

`for` loops over a list:
  for p in [[-25, 95, 25], [25, 95, 25], [-25, 95, 175], [25, 95, 175]]:
      beam = beam - translate(p, slug)

`while` (use sparingly — worker has an iteration cap):
  while count < hole_n:
      ...
      count = count + 1

`if` / `else` with boolean operators &&, ||, !:
  if z > half_len && count != 0:
      beam = beam - translate([0, 95, z], big_slug)
  else:
      beam = beam - translate([0, 95, z], small_slug)

`module` — reusable parameterised geometry; MUST end with `return <shape>`:
  module hole_slug(bolt_r, csink_r, depth=10):
      through = rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=depth + 4, r=bolt_r, center=true))
      csink   = translate([0, depth/2 - 2, 0], rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=5, r1=csink_r, r2=bolt_r, center=true)))
      return through + csink

  slug = hole_slug(4, 7)

`loft:` block — sections at successive Z planes:
  body = loft:
      z=0:   oval(58, 34)
      z=40:  oval(66, 40)
      z=78:  oval(60, 36)
      z=110: oval(34, 18)

Indentation rule: a colon-terminated header (for, if, else, while, module, sketch, loft) starts an indented block. Don't mix tabs and spaces.

§3 — Viewports & coordinate frame

The CAD panel is Z-UP (matching build123d / FreeCAD / SolidWorks native frames): +X is right, +Y is depth (into the screen in iso), +Z is up. The default cylinder() axis is +Z, so a cylinder's "top end" sits at +Z. The default sketch plane is XY (floor), and `extrude(profile, length)` extrudes along +Z — meaning a sketch+extrude T-beam stands on its END with length vertical. That's not a bug, it's the build123d sketch-plane convention being explicit: use it intentionally, and consider rotate([90,0,0], extrude(...)) if you want a horizontal beam.

Wide layout (md/lg/xl) is a 2×2 grid: top/front/right (orthographic OUTLINE x-ray — not shaded 3D renders) + iso (shaded). Narrow layout has ONE switchable view via the projection dropdown. Pane semantics:
- Top   : looks down -Z onto the XY plane. Holes through a cube along +Z appear as CIRCLES here. X right, Y up on screen.
- Front : looks toward +Y from -Y; the XZ plane fills the view. X right, Z up on screen.
- Right : looks toward -X from +X; the YZ plane fills the view. Y right, Z up on screen.
- Iso   : orbited perspective, Z up.

Trust iso for "did the geometry build right," ortho for dimensions/symmetry. When you say "top of the part" to the user, you mean +Z.

§4 — Talking via edge annotations (USER → agent first)

Every evaluated solid has stable indexed edges, and there are TWO label channels:

A. User-authored labels (the user clicks edges in the panel and types notes)
   When the user references "the edges I labeled" (or "pinned"/"tagged"/"marked"/"selected"), they mean these. Call minerva_cad_list_user_labels FIRST. It returns {labels: [{edge_id, text, ...}], count}. Operate on every edge_id in the list — do NOT rely on minerva_cad_get_selected_edge (that returns ONLY the most recent click, not the whole set the user has been pinning). If count==0, then the user has not labeled anything; fall back to get_selected_edge or ask which edges they mean.

B. Agent-authored labels (you label edges so the user can answer "which one?")
   When you and the user need to disambiguate edges, call minerva_cad_list_edges_live, pick candidates, label with minerva_cad_annotate_edges using readable labels ("A", "B", "C"), and ask. The user may then click an edge — read minerva_cad_get_selected_edge for that single click. Clear stale labels with minerva_cad_clear_edge_annotations before the next set.

Edge indices from either channel feed fillet/chamfer in the DSL directly.

§5 — Starting from scratch

No editor open? Spawn one:
  minerva_create_plugin_editor {plugin_id: "cad", editor_item_id: "new_mcad", tab_title: "<descriptive>"}

Returns {editor_name, text_editor_name, buffer_path}. The render panel and the text editor share one DocumentBuffer — passing either name to minerva_doc_* hits the same buffer. No file path until Save-As.

To author or rewrite source:
- minerva_doc_write {editor_name, text: "<full new .mcad source>"}
NEVER minerva_doc_edit on a CAD editor — string-replace doesn't apply to plugin-scene documents.

To read source:
- minerva_doc_read {editor_name} → {text, last_eval, ...}.

To save:
- First save (anonymous → disk): minerva_doc_save {editor_name, path: "<full path>"}.
- After binding: minerva_doc_save {editor_name}.

§6 — Verifying success (automatic, no polling)

minerva_doc_write on a CAD editor is SYNCHRONOUS with the worker eval: the tool reply already contains last_eval populated. Read last_eval.status from the doc_write reply:

- ok        — geometry rendered. last_eval has vertex_count, edge_count, etc. Tell the user what you built.
- error     — worker rejected the DSL. The MCP reply has success=false; surface last_eval.error_kind and last_eval.error_message verbatim. Common causes: OpenSCAD habits (§0), unknown identifiers, sketch block missing variable bindings, indentation drift.
- timeout   — worker didn't reply within 30s. Suggest simplifying.
- cancelled — preempted by a newer evaluate (rare).
- empty     — source was whitespace-only.

NEVER tell the user "done" without reading last_eval.status. The reply is the canonical truth.

Cold-start note: the first eval after Minerva starts can take ~10s (worker process spinup). Don't worry if a single doc_write seems slow — subsequent calls are fast.

Ground before authoring. When you're about to subtract holes/features from existing geometry — or you're combining primitives whose origin conventions might not all match — call minerva_cad_get_mesh_info FIRST and read the bounding_box. The bbox is the single source of truth for "where is the part?" and "what are its extents?". Place children with bbox.min and bbox.max as anchors, not assumed-symmetric coords like [-x/2, x/2]. The cube() corner-at-origin convention bites this exact pattern: a cube(25,25,25) sits in [0,0,0]→[25,25,25], so a hole grid centered around the origin will MISS most of the cube.

§7 — Worked examples (canonical — these are known to evaluate)

10 mm-diameter sphere:
  result = sphere(5)

T-beam (extruded structural section):
  height = 100
  width = 80
  thickness = 10
  length = 100

  sketch:
      flange = rect(width, thickness) center at point(0, height - thickness / 2)
      web    = rect(thickness, height - thickness) center at point(0, (height - thickness) / 2)
      profile = flange + web

  beam = extrude(profile, length)

T-beam with countersunk holes (module + for + CSG subtraction):
  height = 100
  width = 80
  thickness = 10
  length = 200

  sketch:
      flange = rect(width, thickness) center at point(0, height - thickness / 2)
      web    = rect(thickness, height - thickness) center at point(0, (height - thickness) / 2)
      profile = flange + web

  beam = extrude(profile, length)

  module hole_slug(bolt_r, csink_r, depth=10):
      through = rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=depth + 4, r=bolt_r, center=true))
      csink   = translate([0, depth/2 - 2, 0], rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=5, r1=csink_r, r2=bolt_r, center=true)))
      return through + csink

  slug = hole_slug(4, 7)

  for p in [[-25, 95, 25], [25, 95, 25], [-25, 95, 175], [25, 95, 175]]:
      beam = beam - translate(p, slug)

Lofted shell body (organic profile + shell op):
  body = loft:
      z=0:   oval(58, 34)
      z=40:  oval(66, 40)
      z=78:  oval(60, 36)
      z=110: oval(34, 18)

  shell body, 1.8

When the user asks for something close to one of these, START by adapting the matching example — don't synthesise from scratch. Confirm the build via §6, then iterate.

§8 — Exporting to STL / STEP / 3MF

Use minerva_cad_export {editor_name, format, path} to write the current model to disk. The tool resolves the editor's source via DocumentRegistry and runs a fresh evaluation in the worker — you do NOT need to read or pass the source yourself.

Formats:
- 'stl'       → binary STL (build123d default; ASCII is not exposed). Best for slicers, mesh consumers.
- 'step' / 'stp' → STEP AP214 (OCCT default schema). Best for handing off to other CAD tools (Fusion, SolidWorks, FreeCAD).
- '3mf'       → 3MF via build123d Mesher. Modern slicer format, units + colour aware.

Path rules: absolute as-is; ~-prefixed paths expand; bare relative paths resolve against the user's home directory.

Return shape on success: {success: true, path, bytes_written, format}. Surface the path back to the user verbatim — they may want to grab the file. On a parse/translate error the tool returns {success: false, error: 'cad_export_failed (kind=parse|translate): ...'} with the worker's verbatim message; treat it the same way you treat doc_write last_eval errors (§6).

Do NOT use the DSL `export <name> "file.stl"` statement — it parses cleanly but the worker does not flush export targets during cad.evaluate. minerva_cad_export is the only path that actually writes a file.

§9 — Visual verification: minerva_cad_snapshot

TRIGGER: When the user complains about how the model LOOKS ("that's not right", "the chamfers all look the same", "holes are off", "can't tell", "still wrong" — ANY visual comment), your FIRST action is minerva_cad_snapshot, NOT minerva_doc_write. You cannot fix a visual problem you cannot see. Bumping constants without seeing the result wastes the user's time and almost always produces another visually-identical wrong answer.

If you have vision capability, call minerva_cad_snapshot {editor_name, view?: "iso"|"top"|"front"|"right"|"active", return_base64?: true} to SEE the model. Use this any time text-only inspection (mesh_info, list_edges) won't disambiguate what went wrong — e.g. "are the holes on the cube or floating off it?", "do the chamfers look different from each other?". Set return_base64=true to receive the PNG inline; otherwise the tool writes to disk under user://cad_snapshots/ and you get the path back.

Narrow vs wide layout: in NARROW layout only the visible single pane is rendering, so view="top"/"front"/"right" while the projection dropdown is on something else returns null with kind "not rendering". Use view="active" (whatever pane is currently shown), or ask the user to switch the panel to wide layout. The tool internally awaits one frame_post_draw, so cold-start nulls no longer reach you — if you DO get a non-cold-start null error, retrying with the same view will NOT help.

Do NOT retry minerva_cad_snapshot with identical args after a not-rendering failure. The system warns after 3 identical failures; treat that warning as a hard stop. Tell the user what you can't see and propose either switching layout or interpreting the geometry numerically (mesh_info bbox, list_edges).

§10 — Reading the user's intent precisely

CAD asks are often ambiguous in ways that produce visually identical wrong answers. Two patterns bite repeatedly:

(a) QUANTIFIER AMBIGUITY. "Give each hole a larger chamfer" has two readings:
  - Reading A: every hole gets a (uniform) chamfer that is larger than baseline.
  - Reading B: each hole gets a DIFFERENT chamfer, varying across the grid.
Reading B is signalled by words like "each", "different", "varied", "vary", "a gradient of", "per-hole". Reading A is signalled by "all the holes", "uniformly", "a bigger chamfer overall". When ambiguous, STATE YOUR READING in your reply: "I'm reading this as a uniform chamfer increase — every hole gets the same larger size. If you meant varying chamfers per hole, say so and I'll parameterise the module on chamfer_r."

Reading B requires the per-iteration variable to actually VARY. A module called once and translated to many positions produces identical-shape copies — translation is rigid, it does not reshape. To get per-iteration variation you must either: (i) make the module take args and call it with different values per position, or (ii) compute per-iteration values inline.

(b) PUSHBACK ESCALATION. If the user says the result "looks the same", "is still wrong", "didn't change", "all look identical" — DO NOT just bump the same constants and rewrite. That is the failure mode: three tiny edits that all evaluate cleanly and look identical because the underlying ambiguity was never resolved.

When pushed back on a visual result, do EXACTLY ONE of:
  1. Snapshot first (§9) to see what they are seeing. If the snapshot confirms the issue, the geometry is wrong; reason about WHY before rewriting.
  2. Ask which reading they meant. "Do you want them all the same size but bigger, or each hole a DIFFERENT size?" One sentence.

If you find yourself about to call minerva_doc_write a second time after a visual complaint, with the same module structure and slightly different constants — STOP. You are in the failure mode. Snapshot or ask first.

§11 — fillet/chamfer: ALWAYS batch, NEVER chain

OCCT (the B-Rep kernel under build123d) does NOT have stable edge identifiers across topology changes. Every `fillet` and `chamfer` operation deletes the original sharp edge and adds new arc edges; OCCT's internal edge table is rebuilt and `shape.edges()` returns edges in a different order. The MCAD edge registry is just `1..N` over that traversal — so after a single fillet, every other edge id has shifted.

Consequence: writing four sequential fillet statements applies the FIRST fillet to the right edge, but the second/third/fourth statements reference ids that no longer mean what you intended. You will silently fillet the wrong edges (often top edges instead of vertical corners). The DSL evaluates cleanly, the geometry is wrong, and the user has to spot it visually.

ALWAYS use the list form when filleting or chamfering more than one edge:

  fillet  part, [1, 3, 6, 20], r=2
  chamfer part, [4, 8, 12, 16], d=0.5

Both list-form variants resolve ALL ids against the same pre-fillet registry, then call OCCT once. Stable IDs from start to finish.

If you find yourself about to emit a second `fillet` (or `chamfer`) statement on the SAME shape in the SAME doc_write — STOP. Combine the edge ids into a single list. The single-edge form exists only for the genuine one-off case (single corner, single edge); using it more than once per shape per doc_write is a bug.

(Edge ids are still unstable across SEPARATE doc_write calls — between calls the worker re-evaluates from scratch. Always re-list edges via minerva_cad_list_edges_live before each new authoring turn; never reuse ids from a previous turn.)

§12 — Reference meshes: mesh()

`mesh("path")` places an existing mesh file (.glb/.gltf now; .obj/.stl as they land) in the CAD world as REFERENCE geometry. It is a pose, not a solid:

- The worker never opens the file. It records the path exactly as you wrote it, the units and up-axis, and the composed 4x4 transform. The panel resolves the path relative to the saved .mcad document and loads it.
- translate / rotate / scale / mirror compose onto a reference in statement order, exactly as they do on a solid. scale() on a reference must be UNIFORM and non-zero — scale([2,2,2], ...) is fine, scale([1,2,1], ...) is an error naming the reference — because a non-uniform scale turns the file's holes into ellipses, which have no diameter for a measurement to report. translate([10,0,0], rotate([0,0,90], mesh("a.glb"))) is NOT the same placement as rotate([0,0,90], translate([10,0,0], mesh("a.glb"))).
- Nothing else may touch it. a - mesh(...), a + mesh(...), fillet, chamfer, shell, extrude, loft and export on a reference are all errors that name the reference. You cannot cut a solid against a reference, and you cannot reverse a mesh into DSL. If the user asks for either, say so plainly rather than emitting DSL that fails.
- Bind it to a name. Only a named top-level binding is reported to the panel: write board = mesh("main.glb"), never a bare mesh("main.glb") line.
- A reference contributes NO edges. Edge ids still come only from the B-Rep solids, so adding a mesh() line never renumbers the ids you got from minerva_cad_list_edges_live.
- Units and up default by format, because the formats differ: .glb/.gltf default to units="m", up="y" (the glTF spec's own frame); every other extension defaults to units="mm", up="z". Pass units= (mm/cm/m/in) and up= (x/y/z) only when you know the file disagrees with its format's convention.

A document may contain nothing but references — that evaluates cleanly with an empty B-Rep, so importing a board before modelling anything around it is normal.

The owner has a GUI route to the same line: "Import mesh…" in the CAD panel opens a file picker filtered to the loadable formats and appends one refN = mesh("...") line to the document, spelled relative to the saved .mcad. There is no import tool for you, and none is coming: your parity for that action is minerva_doc_write on the same document — append the line yourself, in the same form. In a document that has never been saved the path has to be absolute (the panel warns about it); tell the user to save the .mcad beside the mesh if the pair has to travel.

§13 — Measuring a reference mesh: hypothesise, then verify

A reference is FOREIGN geometry. Nothing tells you where its holes are, and a picture of it will not tell you either — pixels are not millimetres. The measurement verbs give you numbers, and they are built around one rule: a fit is a hypothesis, a gauge is a measurement.

The workflow, in order:
1. minerva_cad_references — what is mounted, where it is posed, what its nodes bound. Start here; it is cheap and it names the references and nodes the other verbs take.
2. minerva_cad_find_holes — every hole, measured. Read dia_mm AND gauge_dia_mm: dia_mm is the circle the tessellation's vertices lie on (the drill the designer asked for), gauge_dia_mm is the largest pin the gauge's rays allow (the chord across the facets, always slightly smaller — a 3.2 mm drill exported as a 64-gon gauges 3.18). Read gauge_bounded: false means no wall was found inside the search bound, so gauge_dia_at_least_mm is a floor and there is no measured diameter. Quote the one the question is about, and say which it is. Read `through` before saying a hole goes through: a blind pocket has exactly the same wall as a through hole and only the ray test tells them apart. Read `verified`: false means the fit was not confirmed by the gauge and the number is a guess.
3. minerva_cad_find_cylinders kind=convex — bosses, standoffs and pins, the same way.
4. minerva_cad_gauge — the direct question: will THIS pin, at THIS place, go in? A gauge that does not fit tells you where it touched, which is the answer to 'why will this screw not go in'. Every gauge and every hole verification is RAY-SAMPLED — 24 azimuths at each of 5 stations along the pin — not a volumetric proof, so 'it fits' means no ray met anything: a rib, a burr or a chamfer standing between two rays can be missed (15° of arc is 1.3 mm of wall at a 5 mm radius). Say 'gauged, not proven' when the answer matters, and gauge again at a size or a place that would catch what you doubt. When the pin stands in open air nothing bounds it: the reply says clearance_bounded false and reports clearance_at_least_mm, which is the search bound and not a distance to anything.
5. minerva_cad_probe — turn a pixel of a snapshot into a position in millimetres.
5b. minerva_cad_get_selected_reference — what the user CLICKED. See §14.
6. minerva_cad_view_overlay then minerva_cad_snapshot — when you do want a picture, put a millimetre grid and the world axes in it first, and use the returned px_per_mm (orthographic panes only) to read it.

Every position comes back in BOTH frames: {world, local}. `local` is the reference's own converted frame — millimetres and Z-up, with the mesh() pose taken back off. The file's own units and up-axis have already been applied, so these are the numbers you write into the DSL: the pose is already in the mesh() line. `world` is the posed scene — that is what you compare against the evaluated solid and against other references. Mixing them up puts geometry in the wrong place with no error message.

The first measurement on a newly loaded file does the segmentation and builds the colliders. That work is SYNCHRONOUS and runs on the panel's main thread: on a very large mesh (a hundred thousand triangles or more) the first minerva_cad_find_holes or minerva_cad_find_cylinders can take several seconds, and the whole app is unresponsive for them — so is a ray-grid fallback at a fine pitch_mm. Warn the user before the first call on a big file, and pass `node` to segment one node instead of all of them. After that the result is cached until the file changes, so ask as many questions as you need. Measurement never alters the reference, and there is no verb that cuts geometry against one — if the user wants a pocket that matches a scanned part, model it from the numbers you measured.

§14 — The user's click is your seed

A reference mesh has no names you and the user share. "This bracket", "that hole", "the tall post" mean nothing to a verb that takes a node name and a diameter. The panel's wide sidebar lists every reference and every node inside it, and a left click in any view selects the node under the cursor and the point on its surface. minerva_cad_get_selected_reference hands you exactly that: the reference, the node, the surface point in both frames, the node's bounds, and the fitted hole the point fell inside if it fell into one. A node is identified by its PATH from the file root ("Assembly/Bracket/Body"), because foreign assemblies reuse leaf names freely; every node= filter accepts either the path (one node) or the bare leaf name (every node carrying it), and a filter that matches nothing is an error listing the nodes there are.

When the user says "this" or "that" about a reference, read the selection FIRST. Then measure that node by name (every measurement verb takes `node`), and quote the numbers back with the node's name so the user can see you are looking at the same thing. If nothing is selected, the reply lists the mounted references — either ask the user to click, or use minerva_cad_select_reference to point at one yourself, which highlights it in their sidebar.

An annotation can be stuck to that point: the cad/point anchor stores the point in the reference's own frame, so re-posing the mesh() line moves every annotation on it, and deleting the line marks them stale instead of stranding them. Edge selection is untouched by any of this — edges belong to the evaluated solid, nodes belong to the references, and both selections stay set at once.
